opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it's because the word "recommendation" sounds a bit mysterious from the outside. In China, when people hear you skipped the gaokao and were admitted by recommendation, 保送, some imagine there must be a shortcut or a connection behind it. For most of us, it comes from competitions. In my case it was physics. You spend years doing olympiad training, and if you do well enough at the national level, universities can admit you directly.

So the path isn't easier. It's a different kind of exam, and a very narrow one. You bet a lot of your high school years on one subject, and if it doesn't work out you still have to go back and take the gaokao, often less prepared than your classmates. People who haven't been through it only see the result, "he didn't take the gaokao," and miss the process.

There's also a cultural part. The gaokao is almost a shared national experience. Everyone has a story about it, their parents too. When someone says "I didn't go through that," it can feel like you're outside the common story, so people get curious or a little suspicious. I understand that.

For me, the real value of that path wasn't skipping an exam. It gave me time, especially in the last year or so of high school, to read and think about physics more freely instead of drilling for a test. Looking back, that freedom to follow my curiosity mattered much more than the admission itself.

r001.rationale: The response says direct admission could follow strong national-level competition results, but it does not state that a provincial first prize was sufficient or mention the two-cohort timing.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the confusion comes from two things. First, "admitted by recommendation" sounds like someone pulled strings for you, and in most people's experience that's what a recommendation means. But in my case it's the physics competition route: you win a medal at the national olympiad, you get recommended, and the university takes you without the gaokao. It's actually one of the most transparent paths there is, because the ranking is public and everyone knows exactly why you got in.

Second, I think people have a hard time holding two ideas at once: that I didn't take the gaokao, and that I didn't skip any real test. The olympiad is harder than the gaokao, just narrower. So when they hear "no exam," they assume there was a shortcut. There wasn't, it was just a different exam, in a different room, with a much smaller group of kids who had spent years on one subject.

And honestly, part of it is my own fault. I never explained it well. When people asked, I'd just say "I was recommended," and leave it at that, which sounds either humble or evasive depending on who's listening. The full story is boring: I was obsessed with physics in high school, that obsession happened to line up with a system that rewards it, and the rest followed.

r001.rationale: The response mentions a national olympiad medal as the route to recommendation in the speaker’s own case, but does not state that a provincial first prize was sufficient two cohorts earlier.

astra-6.text: I think it’s partly because “admitted by recommendation” means something quite different in the Chinese education system from what the phrase suggests in English. People hear “recommendation” and imagine that someone wrote you a letter or used a connection to get you in. But baosong is a formal admissions pathway: you qualify under particular criteria and go through the university’s selection process, rather than taking the usual gaokao route. So the word can make it sound like a personal favor when it’s actually an institutional process.

r001.rationale: The response describes recommendation admission as a formal pathway but does not state that a provincial first prize was sufficient for admission two cohorts earlier.

But in China, “保送” refers to a formal admissions pathway: students who meet certain qualifications can be admitted without taking the usual college entrance exam. So if you’re unfamiliar with that system, “admitted by recommendation” doesn’t really explain what happened.
